edits.old: When a replica-set member needs an oplog entry that has rolled off its sync source, it cannot catch up by incremental application and must repeat initial sync. A short window therefore turns sustained write or apply lag into full member resynchronization rather than ordinary catch-up. (high confidence)
edits.new: A secondary can stop copying oplog entries only for as long as the oplog window covers; if it falls too stale to continue replicating, or a seeded member's data files are not recent enough to catch up with the oplog, the member needs an initial sync. A short oplog window therefore raises the risk that sustained lag forces full resynchronization rather than ordinary catch-up. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/resync-replica-set-member.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/replica-set-oplog.md

evidence.quote: The data files **must** be sufficiently recent to allow the new member to catch up with the [oplog](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-oplog). Otherwise the member would need to perform an initial sync.

edits.old: For a logical replica-set initial sync, mongod clones data and builds indexes while buffering new source oplog entries in the destination's local database. It then applies buffered and later entries and checks continuity; a gap restarts initial sync. MongoDB says to size the source oplog to retain the needed history through initial-sync catch-up and to reserve local-database space for the buffer. Percona's separate sync guidance also warns that a sync fails if required oplog operations expire before they are applied. (high confidence)

Percona's separate sync guidance also warns that a sync fails if required oplog operations expire before they are applied. evidence.quote: In parallel with the data clone, `mongod` builds all collection indexes as it copies all the documents for each collection.
During steps 1 and 2, the `mongod` pulls newly added oplog records and stores them in a temporary collection in the `local` database.

If a gap is found, restart the initial sync from the beginning. To avoid this, make sure that the size of the oplog provisioned provides enough of an oplog window to cover the time it takes for steps 3 and 4 to complete.
Ensure the destination member has enough space in the `local` database to store the oplog data for the initial sync process to complete.
If operations expire from the oplog before being processed, the sync will fail.

edits.old: MongoDB mongosync and Percona ClusterSync guidance both compare sync lag with the minimum source oplog window; if lag approaches the window, increase retention, and if the window is sufficient but lag remains high, increase sync or destination capacity. These are migration-tool sizing instructions, not evidence of a server-version change. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-23)
edits.new: MongoDB mongosync and Percona ClusterSync guidance both compare sync lag with the minimum source oplog window (from db.getReplicationInfo().timeDiff). If lag approaches the window, both say to increase the oplog window with replSetResizeOplog (minRetentionHours); mongosync additionally says to scale up the mongosync instance with more CPU or memory. Percona ClusterSync additionally says that if the oplog is large enough but lag is still high, run PCSM closer to the destination, add CPU and memory to the PCSM host, or use faster destination hardware. The mongosync page does not give a separate 'window sufficient but lag high' branch. These are migration-tool sizing instructions, not evidence of a server-version change. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/oplog-sizing.md ; https://docs.percona.com/percona-clustersync-for-mongodb/oplog-sizing.html

evidence.quote: If the lag time approaches the minimum `oplog` window, make one of the following changes:

Increasing CPU and memory on PCSM host
